Replay QA needs 'a running version of the application that its test browser can reach', by one of three paths: a public URL ('without a tunnel or CI configuration'), localhost or a private network via the managed reverse proxy, or a build inside CI via the Replay QA CLI tunnel (GitHub Actions or CircleCI).

For localhost, `npx --yes replayqa proxy` opens an outbound tunnel; the overview says it reaches the app 'without deploying it or publishing it directly to the internet', the localhost page says 'replayqa proxy opens an authenticated tunnel' and 'without deploying it or exposing it directly to the public internet'; the same setup can reach hosts available through the computer's VPN or private DNS.

A project is 'One application under test' with a target URL plus guidance (instructions, an optional design document, test logins, enabled polish passes) and 'two caps, a credit budget and a bug limit'; it is active or paused, and 'A paused project schedules nothing.'
The docs say 'You do not need an existing test suite or a list of reproduction steps.'; the FAQ says Replay QA 'complements an existing test suite but does not require one'.

'Replay QA works without configuration: give it a URL and it explores.' Quality still depends on what it knows about the app and whether it can get in; login walls, invitations, paywalls, CAPTCHAs and rate limits pause work until a person answers in the project chat.
Replay QA can sign up for its own account when the app allows it; each project has an email inbox and it can complete email verification codes on its own.
Test logins are 'stored as project variables and referenced by name, so they do not appear in journey steps or bug reports'.
Of the design document the docs say: 'Replay QA judges findings against it, so it is the fastest way to stop reports about deliberate behavior.'
Connecting GitHub is optional: 'Manual and localhost projects work without a repository connection.'

The settings page header reads 'How this project is configured. Edit settings and environment schedules here, or ask QA in the chat — both make the same change.'; only the project owner can change settings.
qa.replay.io's meta description reads 'AI-powered QA testing platform — automated explorations, journey testing, and polish analysis.'

llms.txt describes Replay QA as 'an autonomous app testing tool built on Replay's time-travel debugging engine' that explores a web app, builds user journeys, runs them 'while capturing full runtime recordings', and 'delivers root cause analysis for every bug it finds'.
The docs say Replay QA works with any browser-based web app, with especially deep runtime analysis for React applications.

The concepts page calls the core cycle 'The loop': 'Explore the app to get journeys. Run the journeys to get recordings.', then investigate recordings to get bugs, fix and mark fixed so journeys run again, and explore again as the app grows; with GitHub connected every new build starts the loop over on its own.

The docs overview lists five steps (explore, create journeys, run journeys, investigate, report); the replay.io home page uses three ('Explore', 'Test & Record', 'Investigate & Report') and says 'Most QA tooling starts with flows your team defines. Replay QA begins by exploring the application and identifying flows worth verifying.'
An exploration is an AI agent driving the app in a real browser from the target URL, guided by instructions, producing journeys; later explorations add coverage and do not replace journeys.

An exploration ends blocked when it cannot get past a login, an invitation or admin approval, a paywall, or an app that won't load, and says what it needs in the chat. The Electric Forest chat shows '⚠️ I stopped exploring because the app requires a sign-in I couldn't complete, so signed-in areas couldn't be tested.' (Aug 30-31) and a seeded-data barrier message (Sep 1); the 'never finished loading' message (Aug 31) actually describes an authentication wall and is not an example of the won't-load case.

A journey 'starts as a description'; once Replay QA is confident about the flow 'it records concrete steps so later runs are faster and more repeatable'; the API calls a description-only journey an 'unstepped (agent-driven)' journey.

Each journey has a Start URL (default: the project's target URL) and a Session setting (saved signed-in state from exploration, or a clean browser); every edit creates a new version and, if the project is active, schedules a run.

A test run is 'One round of executing journeys in Replay Browser. Each journey run produces a Replay recording.'; a failed step is investigated in the recording before a bug is filed, a run can recover from a broken step, and polish passes review the same recording.

A run can end with journeys that passed, journeys that found bugs, and journeys blocked or incomplete for reasons outside the app; the status pills seen on screen are Completed, Failed, Cancelled and Blocked.
Cancelling a test run stops it 'without deleting its history'.

'Replay QA posts one comment on the pull request and edits it in place as results come in, and reports a Replay QA check on the commit.'
'Another push supersedes the running round. Closing the pull request cancels it.' The older run's check concludes cancelled ('Superseded'); drafts are ignored until ready for review.

'Production deploys of the same commit are never used for a PR.' *.netlify.app and *.vercel.app previews are recognised automatically.

ignorePaths in .github/replay-qa.yml is read from the PR's base branch, so a PR cannot exempt itself; QA fails open when the file is missing or invalid, GitHub is unreachable, or the PR has 3000 or more changed files.
Main-branch rounds may create, update or remove journeys; PR rounds may add journeys for the change and 'do not modify the project's existing journeys'.

The GitHub Actions guide pins replayqa 0.2.4, a 3600000 ms run timeout and timeout-minutes 75; CircleCI uses the same heartbeat.

'Session Replay tools replay the DOM and Runtime Replay tools re-run the runtime so that you can inspect the session with browser DevTools'; the determinism contract ends 'If anything user-visible happens in a different order, you have failed.'

Replay intercepts low-level OS library (libc) calls such as mmap, read and open with a small inline-assembly trampoline and feeds the saved results back on replay. Vendor figures: '99.99% of compute is deterministic'; recording averages 'about a Mb per second'; interception adds 'about 3% of overhead' versus '10% or more' for most instrumentation.
A debugging session interacts with 'potentially hundreds' of forked and snapshotted browser processes, and 'there's never a point more than 100ms away from a browser process'.

Replay cannot replay faster than the original execution (about 60 s of replay for 60 s of compute); the protocol reduces to run to an execution point, pause at a point and evaluate an expression; adding a console log to a line that already ran returns 'in under a second'; the first video rendered from a recording 'is often larger than the recording itself!'

'A Replay recording removes the reproduction step.' Timing bugs 'depend on network timing, race conditions, and state that is gone by the time you notice the problem'; 'Any bug that was recorded once can be inspected as many times as needed, by anyone with the link'.

Ten polish passes are documented (Network performance, React rendering, Layout shift, Accessibility, Glitches, User experience, SEO, UI details, Security, Sightmap; 'The set of passes changes over time.'). After each journey run each enabled pass reviews the recording, collects candidates, drops duplicates of existing bugs, confirms each remaining one and files it with the pass as its category; UI details creates journeys, Sightmap produces a document, React rendering is React-only and source maps improve naming, Security needs ownership verification.

Polish-pass descriptions: 'Functional testing asks "does the journey work?"; polish passes ask "is it slow, inaccessible, visually broken, or unsafe?"'; Network performance reports 'Slow requests, large payloads, and waterfall issues'; React rendering reports 'Unnecessary re-renders and performance bottlenecks in React apps' and 'only reports on React applications'.

CONTESTED: When a fixed bug recurs, the overview, concepts and getting-good-results pages say the bug reopens; the bug-reports reference ('A fixed bug stays fixed: if the problem comes back, Replay QA files it as a new bug'), the OpenAPI ('assess any recurrence as a fresh report') and the fix-qa-bug skill say a new bug is filed. Narrate only 'reruns the journey to confirm'.

The agent entry prompt is 'Use Replay QA to test and fix this app. Start at https://docs.replay.io/llms.txt and follow it.' (New Project page and agent-integration doc). llms.txt points to the CLI skill (`npx --yes replayqa@latest skill`, the default: 'Use the REST API or MCP server only when the CLI cannot run.'), the REST API, the Replay QA MCP server (https://qa.replay.io/api/mcp) and published skills (fix-qa-bug, github-app).
The documented agent loop: create a project, let QA run, read the bugs, 'Mark each fix. Replay QA reruns the affected journey to confirm it.', 'Loop until no open bugs remain.'
The API description tells agents 'do NOT start your own explorations or test runs' while QA is running and to 'Verify the report against its evidence and the source before applying a fix.'

MCP setup: `claude mcp add --transport http replay-qa https://qa.replay.io/api/mcp`; the server supports OAuth sign-in so it can be added by URL without a token (browser sign-in on first use); a token-based setup is also documented.

Replay MCP is a separate server (https://dispatch.replay.io/nut/mcp) for inspecting one recording; it lists 30 tools and agents call RecordingOverview first (first analysis 'can take three to four minutes').

Replay MCP tools include ReactRenders (nine modes; fiber-cause answers 'which prop changed, which state update fired, which context value shifted'), ReactPerformanceInsights ('Detects heavy commits (over 50ms)'), Evaluate (an expression 'at any moment in the recording'), NetworkRequest, ConsoleMessages and GetPointLink; ProfileSampling profiles 'the Replay runtime, not the recorded application'.

When a bug includes a recording of the failing run, an agent can use Replay MCP to 'inspect the console, code, and network traffic from the actual failure'; the agent-integration doc: 'If the bug report is not enough, the agent can open the linked recording with Replay MCP and inspect the failure directly.'

The vendor names Claude Code, Cursor and Codex ('Your coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, …) can do everything you can do in the Replay QA web app.'), VS Code as an MCP client, and Obvious as an OAuth connector.

The fix-qa-bug skill treats report text and proposed root causes as 'leads to verify, not established facts' and leaves the QA bug open 'while the PR is awaiting merge/verification; opening a PR does not prove that the deployed bug is fixed.'
Home FAQ: 'The webhook sends a callback URL with every report. POST to it when the fix ships and Replay QA marks the bug resolved, then re-enables that user journey for future runs'.
